Matt Pierce's June Newsletter Indiana ranks 45th for support of public education, Interim Study Committees and more. Rep. Matt Pierce Jun 30, 2026 Share Welcome to my monthly newsletter, where I provide legislative updates as your state representative for House District 61. Please reach out to me at h61@iga.in.gov if you have any comments, questions, or concerns. Everyone Should Be Welcome in Indiana Indiana is home to nearly 7 million people who worship in different ways and raise families of every shape. At the start of this month, Indiana’s leaders spent time casting judgment on families and faiths that don’t resemble their own. Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith told Hoosiers it is acceptable to hate again, characterizing our Muslim neighbors as jihadists. The same neighbors are raising their kids and building their lives in our communities. On the first day of June, Gov. Mike Braun declared that a biological nuclear family is “God’s design,” brushing aside single parents, blended families, adoptive families, grandparents raising grandchildren, and households led by two moms or two dads. Our communities are made stronger by the diversity of experiences, traditions, and families that call Indiana home. Every family building a safe, loving home deserves dignity and respect. Hoosier hospitality has always meant taking care of your neighbors and welcoming people as they are. Time spent by the Braun-Beckwith administration policing private lives is time not spent on the issues that matter. F amilies are stretched thin, paying for the basics necessary to maintain their households. Health care, child care and affordable housing are beyond the reach of too many. Hoosiers did not ask for a lecture on who belongs here. They want help making ends meet. I choose to represent every Hoosier family and every faith, not just those approved by Governor Braun or Lt. Governor Beckwith . Indiana Ranks 45th for Public Education Support The Network for Public Education released its 2026 national report card , and Indiana received an “F” ranking. Indiana ranked 45th in the nation for legislative support for public education. This data confirms what those of us who have been fighting for public education in the state legislature have been saying for years. This is a direct consequence of the Statehouse Republicans’ support for voucher s for private schools . Each year, Statehouse Republicans have expanded eligibility for vouchers, siphoning money away from public schools . Vouchers are now universal. Any family, regardless of wealth, can receive a state-funded voucher of $6,100 to $8,300 to cover the cost of private school. There is no income eligibility limit. A billionaire qualifies for a taxpayer-funded voucher. Privatization and disinvestment in our public schools go hand in hand. In the 2024-25 school year, Indiana spent close to $497 million on vouchers , a $58 million increase from the prior school year. The two-year state budget spends more than $1.2 billion on the program. Each dollar in the budget for the voucher program is a dollar less for our public schools. Our communities are feeling the impact. NPE’s report notes Indiana’s poor marks on teacher-student ratios, counselor-student ratios, and the inability to attract prospective teachers to the profession. Each of these is a symptom of chronic underfunding. This report card gives Indiana a failing grade. Around 90% of students choose public schools. As the state legislature enters the next budget cycle, I will advocate for Indiana’s public school system, which serves the majority of our students. My Interim Study Committees Between legislative sessions, interim study committees are assigned topics to study for possible legislation in the coming session. Committees have the opportunity to consider specific issues, analyze recent studies, and decide if legislation should be recommended for consideration by the entire Indiana General Assembly. I am serving on these interim study committees: Artificial Intelligence Task Force Interim Study Committee on Energy, Utilities and Telecommunications Interim Study Committee on Corrections and Criminal Code But I only expect one of these committees will meet. Many of the study committees will not meet this year because they are assigned no topics to study. Republican leaders appear to prefer avoiding talk about challenges facing our state in an election year rather than giving legislators and the public a platform to demand that problems be addressed. The following committees were not assigned any topics to study: Agriculture And Natural Resources Commerce And Economic Development Elections Energy, Utilities, And Telecommunications Environmental Affairs Government Public Safety And Military Affairs Public Policy These task forces and committees created by law were also denied any study topics: Probate Code Study Committee Health Care Cost Oversight Task Force Artificial Intelligence Task Force Child Welfare Task Force Guardianship Code Revision Task Force You can find a full list of topics the legislature is studying here . Rep. Matt Pierce's October Newsletter Rep. Matt Pierce's Newsletter Subscribe Sign in Rep. Matt Pierce's October Newsletter Resources for the SNAP pause, rising child care costs and more. Rep. Matt Pierce Oct 30, 2025 Share Welcome to my monthly newsletter, where I provide legislative updates as your state representative for House District 61. Please reach out to me at h61@iga.in.gov if you have any comments, questions, or concerns Thank You for Coming to My Town Hall Thank you to everyone who attended my recent town hall. This past year has been a tumultuous period for our nation and state. Many are nervous about the current direction of our government and angered by Gov. Braun’s convening of a special session to redraw Congressional districts currently represented by Democrats. While seeing the relentless destruction of the foundations of our democracy can lead to despair and a sense of helplessness, it’s important for everyone who opposes this destruction to come together and show we’re united in preserving our democracy. I enjoyed hearing your thoughts and answering questions about how we can best stop this brazen power grab. I appreciate everyone who took time out of their busy schedules to attend the town hall meeting. Rep. Pierce answers questions from attendees at his recent town hall Trump Admin Pauses SNAP: Here’s Some Resources The Trump administration will halt the distribution of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC) benefits next month due to the government shutdown. Around 600,000 Hoosier families rely on SNAP, and over 150,00 mothers and infants rely on WIC. President Trump said he would use the government shutdown to close “ Democrat programs that we want to close up or we never wanted to happen. ” Regardless of politics, no one in Indiana should go hungry, especially not our children. And this will hit our kids the hardest. More than 69% of Indiana’s SNAP participants are families with children. This lapse in benefits is also coming at a time when our food banks and pantries in Bloomington are stretched thin. Increased need and cuts in federal funding for nonprofits have resulted in fewer resources. If you’re financially able, please consider donating to a pantry or starting a food drive with friends or extended family. Every bit counts during this unprecedented pause in SNAP. If you’re facing food insecurity this month, here are places in Bloomington you can receive food assistance. Please reach out to me at h61@iga.in.gov if you need help finding food assistance. The resources list below is courtesy of Hoosier Hills Food Bank: Redistricting Session Schedule Despite Governor Braun proclaiming a special session to begin on Monday, November 3 rd at noon, House Speaker Todd Huston and President Pro Tempore Rod Bray say the legislature will not convene next week. The legislature can choose to convene at a later time. A 40-day time limit for the legislature to meet in special session and complete its business starts on the November 3 rd date chosen by the Governor. A maximum of 30 meeting days is allowed during the 40-day window for the special session. Former Governor Eric Holcomb called a special session for July 6th in 2022, but the legislature didn’t convene until July 25 of that year and adjourned on August 5th. It’s unclear when the special session will begin. The Organization Day for the next regular session of the General Assembly is already scheduled for November 18 th . Indiana’s Child Care Crisis Parents aren’t surprised by the news that Indiana has a serious child care problem. Ask any Indiana parent, and they’ll explain the difficulties they face. It’s almost impossible to find affordable, quality child care in our state. Child care is hard to find and even harder to afford. In Bloomington, our providers can only serve 62% of kids zero to five. If you do find a child care provider, the cost is another problem. The Indiana average full-time monthly cost for child care is $720 per month for a single child. That number doubles or triples depending on the family’s size. As a result, the majority of our parents are forgoing child care. They’re relying on close friends and family to watch the kids, or they’re leaving employment. Last year, 40% parents left the workforce due to issues with child care. Recent changes in state funding will make the crisis worse. In early September, the Braun Administration slashed provider reimbursement rates for its Child Care Development Fund Vouchers (CCDF). Low-income families use these vouchers to cover the cost of care. Now, child care providers who serve voucher kids aren’t getting adequately reimbursed for their services. It’s an added financial stressor that’s already caused the closure of a few providers across the state. Indiana needs to revamp its child care system to support parents, care for our kids and ensure those who want to work can. This will not only help families, it will pay huge dividends for Hoosier children in the future. Indiana House Democrats will focus on child care reform during the next session. Rep. Pierce and Sen.
